timeline.body: Iran granted British entrepreneur William Knox D'Arcy a 60-year concession covering nearly all of Persia's oil — the deal that would eventually become the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, later BP, extracting wealth on terms Iran had no power to renegotiate.

The CIA and MI6 overthrew Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh after he nationalized Iran's oil industry, reinstalling Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi and ending Iran's most credible experiment with democratic governance.

The US helped establish SAVAK, the Shah's secret police, which became one of the most feared intelligence agencies in the Middle East — torturing and disappearing thousands of dissidents over two decades.

Britain announced its withdrawal from all military bases east of Suez by 1971, leaving a power vacuum in the Persian Gulf that the US filled by arming the Shah as its regional proxy under the Nixon Doctrine.

The Iranian Revolution overthrew the Shah and established an Islamic Republic under Ayatollah Khomeini, ending 25 years of US-backed authoritarian rule and realigning Iran from America's closest Gulf ally to its most committed adversary.

Revolutionary students stormed the US Embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days — an event that hardened American public opinion against Iran for a generation and made diplomacy politically radioactive in Washington.
Iraq invaded Iran with quiet US and Gulf Arab backing, beginning an eight-year war that killed roughly 500,000 people while Western powers supplied arms to both sides.

Israeli jets destroyed Iraq's Osirak nuclear reactor near Baghdad in Operation Opera, establishing the Begin Doctrine: Israel would use preemptive force to prevent any regional rival from acquiring nuclear capability.

Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, and Oman formed the Gulf Cooperation Council — nominally an economic bloc, practically a security pact born from shared fear of revolutionary Iran spreading across the Gulf.
Iran began funding and training Hezbollah in Lebanon, opening the first front of a proxy war with Israel that would eventually span Lebanon, Palestine, Syria, Iraq, and Yemen.

The US Navy launched Operation Earnest Will to escort Kuwaiti oil tankers through the Persian Gulf, the largest naval convoy operation since World War II — openly siding with Iraq while over 400 merchant ships had been attacked in the tanker war.

USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Strait of Hormuz, killing all 290 civilians aboard including 66 children; the US never formally apologized and awarded the ship's captain a Legion of Merit.

George W. Bush named Iran part of an 'Axis of Evil' alongside Iraq and North Korea, collapsing a quiet channel of US-Iran cooperation that had opened after 9/11 when Tehran helped Washington target the Taliban.
Iran and the P5+1 signed the JCPOA nuclear deal in Vienna, trading verifiable limits on uranium enrichment for sanctions relief — the most significant US-Iran diplomatic achievement in 36 years.

Trump unilaterally withdrew the US from the JCPOA and reimposed maximum-pressure sanctions, despite Iran's verified compliance, destroying the diplomatic framework and pushing Iran to resume enrichment beyond deal limits.

A US drone strike at Baghdad Airport assassinated Qasem Soleimani, commander of Iran's Quds Force and architect of its regional proxy network, marking the closest the two countries had come to open war since 1988.
Iran and Israel exchanged direct missile and drone strikes for the first time in their history, shattering the unspoken rule that their decades-long conflict would only be fought through proxies.
Iran and Israel fought a 12-day war involving direct US military participation, transforming a forty-year proxy conflict into an open regional war with American forces engaged on one side.

The Strait of Hormuz narrows to just 24 miles between Iran and Oman — roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passes through it daily, giving Iran a geographic chokepoint that no amount of military spending can relocate.

iran-us-israel-war.label: Iran-US-Israel war: Gulf states weigh military entry, Hormuz blockade tightens

timeline.body: The Federal Aviation Agency was created to manage US airspace after a series of midair collisions — for the next four decades, airport security remained a private affair run by airlines hiring minimum-wage contract screeners.

A wave of hijackings forced the US to introduce the first mandatory airport screening — but airlines, not the government, chose and paid the security companies, creating an obvious conflict between cost-cutting and thoroughness.
Attorney General Benjamin Civiletti issued an opinion that federal employees cannot work during a funding gap, establishing the legal doctrine that turns budget disputes into government shutdowns.

Reagan fired 11,345 striking air traffic controllers and banned them from federal service for life, setting the precedent that essential transportation workers could be disciplined for refusing to work under government-imposed conditions.

A budget standoff between Newt Gingrich's Republican Congress and President Clinton triggered a 21-day shutdown — the longest in US history at that point — furloughing 800,000 federal workers and closing national parks.
On September 11, nineteen hijackers passed through airport checkpoints staffed by private screeners earning roughly $6 an hour with annual turnover rates above 100% at some airports.

Congress passed the Aviation and Transportation Security Act 69 days after 9/11, federalizing all airport screening and creating the TSA — overnight turning 55,000 low-wage contract workers into federal employees with better pay but no right to strike.
The Homeland Security Act merged 22 federal agencies into the new Department of Homeland Security, the largest government reorganization since the Department of Defense was created in 1947.

ICE was stood up inside DHS by merging customs and immigration enforcement functions — an agency born without its own legislative charter, giving successive administrations unusual latitude to redefine its mission.

A 16-day shutdown over Affordable Care Act funding forced TSA screeners to work without pay while Congress continued drawing salaries — the Government Employee Fair Treatment Act guaranteeing back pay for essential workers would not pass for another six years.

The longest government shutdown in US history began over border wall funding, lasting 35 days and leaving 800,000 federal workers — including 51,000 TSA agents — without paychecks through the holidays.

TSA sickout rates hit 10% during the 2018–19 shutdown as unpaid screeners called in absent, producing hour-long security lines at major airports and forcing several terminals to close checkpoints entirely.

Congress passed the Government Employee Fair Treatment Act, guaranteeing back pay to essential workers after a shutdown — but the law does nothing about the weeks or months they must work for free while waiting.
A federal union survey found that 78% of TSA officers were living paycheck to paycheck, meaning even a single missed pay period pushed many toward eviction, missed car payments, or food insecurity.
ICE expanded its presence at domestic airports through the Fugitive Operations program, conducting enforcement actions at terminals — a shift from its original focus on border ports of entry.

TSA screened a record 3.1 billion passengers across US airports, making the agency's 47,000 frontline officers the most visible federal workforce most Americans encounter — and the most exposed when funding lapses.

tsa-ice-dhs-shutdown.label: TSA workers unpaid in second shutdown as ICE militarizes airports
